unit.title: Subjunctive Without a Trigger
unit.subtitle: Quizá, ojalá, que + subjunctive and other independent-clause moods

grammar.title: The subjunctive that stands on its own
grammar.intro: By C2 you know the subjunctive follows triggers like quiero que or dudo que. But educated Spanish also uses it in independent, main clauses — with no subordinating verb at all. Here the mood itself carries the meaning: it signals your attitude, turning a bare statement into doubt, a wish, or a command. Choosing venga over viene is a deliberate act of style.

sections.heading: Quizá(s) / tal vez / acaso: indicative vs. subjunctive
sections.body: Doubt adverbs — quizá(s), tal vez, acaso, posiblemente, probablemente — let you pick the mood, and the choice is meaningful: the subjunctive marks the event as more remote or hypothetical, the indicative treats it as more likely or asserted. Note the split: this only works when the adverb precedes the verb. If it comes after (viene quizá), only the indicative is possible.
conj: Maybe he's coming (I lean toward yes)

ex.es: Tal vez tenga razón, aunque lo dudo.
ex.en: Maybe he's right, though I doubt it.

sections.heading: Ojalá: present vs. imperfect subjunctive
sections.body: Ojalá (from Arabic “would to God”) takes only the subjunctive, never a que before it is required. The tense changes the meaning: present subjunctive = a hope you consider possible; imperfect subjunctive = a wish you see as unlikely or contrary to fact.
conj: If only he had come (impossible now)

ex.en: I hope I pass the exam tomorrow.

ex.es: Ojalá pudiera ayudarte, pero no depende de mí.
ex.en: I wish I could help you, but it's not up to me.

sections.heading: Que + subjunctive as a standalone wish or order
sections.body: A clause opening with que + subjunctive, with no main verb, works as an independent wish, third-person command, or blessing. It reads as if an implicit espero / quiero had been dropped. This is how natives toss out good wishes and delegate tasks.
conj: May it go well for you!

ex.es: Yo no pienso ir; que vayan ellos.
ex.en: I'm not going; let them go.

sections.heading: Quién + imperfect subjunctive: the wistful wish
sections.body: Quién followed by the imperfect subjunctive expresses a longing the speaker knows is out of reach — “if only I could…”. It always refers to the speaker despite the third-person form, and it is emphatic and literary in flavour.

ex.en: If only I were twenty again!
If only one could live without working!

takeaways: Quizá/tal vez + subjunctive = more doubt; + indicative = more likely. After the verb, indicative only.
Ojalá + present subj. = a real hope; + imperfect subj. = an unlikely or impossible wish.
Que + subjunctive alone = an independent wish or third-person command (¡Que te vaya bien!).
Quién + imperfect subjunctive = a wistful, unreachable wish about oneself (¡Quién pudiera!).

mistakes.w: Ojalá que venga mañana… ojalá venga ayer.
mistakes.why: A wish about the past or the unlikely needs the imperfect or pluperfect subjunctive, never the present.
The wistful ‘quién’ wish requires the imperfect subjunctive (pudiera), not the indicative.
An independent wish with ‘que’ takes the subjunctive: vaya, not va.

exercises.prompt: Tal vez ___ razón, pero sinceramente lo dudo mucho.
exercises.prompt_en: Maybe he's right, but honestly I doubt it very much.
exercises.ok: ¡Correcto! La duda marcada pide subjuntivo: tenga.
exercises.no: Because the speaker stresses the doubt (“lo dudo”), the subjunctive fits: tal vez tenga.

exercises.prompt: ___ pudiera ayudarte, pero la decisión no depende de mí.
exercises.prompt_en: I wish I could help you, but the decision isn't up to me.
exercises.ok: ¡Exacto! Ojalá + imperfecto de subjuntivo = deseo poco probable.
exercises.no: The unlikely wish “I wish I could” is Ojalá pudiera; the other adverbs don't express that longing.

exercises.prompt: Build: “I'm not going; let them do it.”
exercises.ok: ¡Perfecto! Que + subjuntivo = mandato de tercera persona.
exercises.no: The standalone “let them” command uses the subjunctive: que lo hagan ellos, not hacen.

exercises.prompt: ¡___ pudiera empezar de cero otra vez! (quién)
exercises.prompt_en: If only I could start over from scratch!
exercises.hint: The wistful wish about oneself starts with this interrogative word.
exercises.no: The longing “if only I could” opens with Quién + imperfect subjunctive: ¡Quién pudiera!

exercises.prompt: Match each independent-clause expression to its meaning.
exercises.ok: ¡Excelente! El modo por sí solo transmite la actitud.

exercises.translation: I hope I pass the exam tomorrow.
exercises.no: It was: “Ojalá apruebe el examen mañana.” (present subjunctive → a real hope).

exercises.scenario: A friend is leaving on a long trip ✈️

lines.speaker: Marta
lines.es: Me voy tres meses a Argentina. ¡Deséame suerte!
lines.en: I'm off to Argentina for three months. Wish me luck!

options.text: ¡Que te vaya muy bien y que disfrutes!
¡Que te va muy bien y que disfrutas!

exercises.no: An independent good wish uses que + subjunctive: “¡Que te vaya bien y que disfrutes!”

exercises.en: If only one could live without working!
exercises.no: Almost — tap “Hear it”, then match the rhythm of “¡Quién pudiera vivir sin trabajar!”

vocab.en: may it go well for you
